1ohnfur:307: This paper proposes a key insight: there is no need to train two separate policy models for the parent RLM and child RLM. By having child RLM rollouts inherit the parent RLM's advantage, a single shared policy can simultaneously play both the parent decomposer and child sub-agent roles. This design avoids the cumbersome pipeline of dual-policy training, while ensuring training stability through GRPO's group-relative advantage computation. A key implementation detail is dividing the child loss by $k_g$ (the number of children) to balance weights, preventing child rollouts from dominating gradient updates when $k_g \gg 1$.

7eu6kh:316: The paper details an important but often overlooked aspect of RLM training: each turn does not share a prefix; the user prompt is re-appended at every turn rather than accumulated into the chat history. This means one trajectory produces N independent training samples instead of one coherent sequence. This is completely different from traditional chat RL, where each trajectory is a full sequence. In RLM, the step-wise structure requires each turn to compute log-prob separately and share the final advantage. This design ensures the original user query is not buried deep in the model's context window, and each turn is re-reminded of its task.
